strengths: Important problem formulation: Extends MLLM spatial reasoning beyond static single images to multi-frame/two-view spatial and dynamic understanding (depth, correspondence, camera motion, object motion, and object size), which is essential for robotics and embodied AI.

Well-designed and scalable data generation pipeline: The data engine thoughtfully tackles challenges in multi-view data synthesis, including overlap-ratio binning to handle long-tailed distributions, BFS-based minimum-coverage-set search for object size perception, and rigid-body clustering on 4D point tracking data to ensure motion diversity.

Significant dataset scale and comprehensive benchmark: Generating over 27M QA pairs across diverse tasks and formats (quantitative coordinates, 3D vectors, continuous metric scalars, multiple-choice), accompanied by a standardized benchmark of 7,800 held-out evaluation samples.

Strong experimental validation and transferability: Multi-SpatialMLLM demonstrates large performance gains over base InternVL models and closed-source proprietary systems (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5, Gemini 2.0). It transfers effectively to zero-shot external spatial benchmarks (BLINK) while maintaining performance on standard VQA benchmarks without catastrophic forgetting.
weaknesses: Predominantly two-frame rather than long/dense multi-frame reasoning: Despite the 'Multi-Frame' framing, almost all tasks and evaluations operate strictly on image pairs (2 views), except for the object size perception search. Testing on multi-view sets (N >= 3) or video sequences would provide stronger support for general multi-frame spatial intelligence.

Limited architectural novelty: The methodology relies entirely on off-the-shelf MLLM architectures (InternVL2) fine-tuned with standard LoRA. While this demonstrates the power of the data, the paper does not explore domain-specific architectural inductive biases (e.g., camera pose embeddings, cross-frame epipolar attention, or explicit 3D geometric representations).

Evaluation metrics could better follow standard vision benchmarks: The 20% relative L2 norm threshold can be sensitive to magnitude (overly strict for near-zero motions and lenient for very large displacements). Reporting standard computer vision metrics (e.g., median translation error in cm, angular error in degrees, and PCK at multiple pixel thresholds for correspondence) would allow clearer comparison with classical 3D vision methods.

Overstated claim regarding 'emergent' spatial understanding: Section 4.3 infers 'emergent abilities' based on a single experiment (multiple-choice visual correspondence with hard distractors) tested across only three checkpoints (8B, 13B, 26B). Given existing literature cautioning against claims of emergence arising from nonlinear evaluation metrics, this claim should be substantially toned down.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely gap in multimodal LLM literature: extending spatial understanding beyond single-image reasoning to multi-view and dynamic multi-frame scenarios (e.g., camera pose change, 3D correspondence, object movement).

Presents a well-engineered and rigorous data generation pipeline leveraging established 3D/4D datasets (ScanNet, TAPVid-3D, ADT, Panoptic Studio). The algorithmic designs—such as overlap-ratio binning, BFS-based minimal coverage set search, and clustering-based rigid body motion segmentation—ensure high-quality and diverse annotations.

Comprehensive scale and task diversity: MultiSPA introduces over 27M samples spanning 26 subtasks and supports diverse referencing (visual dots, coordinates, semantic labels) and diverse output formats (scalars, coordinates, 3D displacement vectors).

Strong empirical performance: Fine-tuning InternVL2 on MultiSPA yields dramatic improvements over base models and frontier proprietary models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5, Gemini 2.0) on both the MultiSPA benchmark and zero-shot splits of the external BLINK benchmark, while retaining standard general VQA performance.

Insightful analysis of multi-task synergy, scaling behavior across data volume and model parameter sizes, and preliminary empirical observations regarding the emergence of fine-grained correspondence discrimination with larger model capacities.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: The approach relies purely on standard LoRA fine-tuning of an off-the-shelf MLLM (InternVL2) using language modeling loss over text tokens. There are no explicit geometric inductive biases, 3D coordinate encodings, or cross-view attention modules introduced into the architecture.

Potential format and domain bias on the MultiSPA benchmark: While evaluation scenes are held out, the benchmark shares the exact prompt templates, synthetic query formulations, and coordinate/metric formatting conventions (e.g., millimeter units, [0, 1000] pixel normalization) with the training data. Baselines, particularly closed-source generalist models, are inherently disadvantaged as they were never instruction-tuned to output exact metric vectors or normalized coordinates in this exact convention.

Overwhelming reliance on two-frame pairs: Despite the title emphasizing 'Multi-Frame', the dataset and experiments are almost entirely restricted to image pairs ($N=2$). True temporal sequences or multi-view reasoning with $\ge 3$ images are minimally explored (only briefly touched in object size perception and qualitative robot demos).

strengths: Addresses a crucial limitation in current MLLM literature: while single-image spatial understanding has been explored recently, multi-frame and dynamic spatial reasoning (depth, 2D/3D visual correspondence, camera movement, and object 3D motion) has been largely overlooked.

Principled data generation engine: The automated pipeline curates training pairs and triplets using ground-truth 3D/4D scans and tracks (ScanNet, TAPVid3D, Aria Digital Twin, Panoptic Studio) rather than noisy monocular estimators. Thoughtful techniques like overlap-ratio binning, BFS minimum-coverage set search, and rigid-body motion clustering ensure diverse and balanced sampling.

Strong empirical performance: Fine-tuning InternVL2 with LoRA yields substantial gains across diverse spatial subtasks, outperforming both base models and leading proprietary models (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.0, Claude-3.5) on the MultiSPA benchmark.

Good transferability and generality: Multi-SpatialMLLM demonstrates zero-shot generalization on the external BLINK benchmark (notably on Visual Correspondence and Multi-View Reasoning splits) while successfully preserving general VQA proficiency on standard benchmarks like POPE, MathVista, and VizWiz.
Insightful analysis on multi-task synergy, scaling behavior across data volume and model parameters, and an engaging demonstration of potential utility as a zero-shot reward annotator for robotics.
weaknesses: Primarily restricted to image pairs: Although titled 'Multi-Frame Spatial Understanding', the vast majority of tasks, data generation formulations, and experiments are conducted strictly on two-view image pairs rather than multi-frame video sequences or dense multi-view scenes.

Limited architectural novelty: The technical contribution lies primarily in data synthesis and curation rather than modeling. The architecture is a vanilla off-the-shelf MLLM (InternVL2) fine-tuned via standard LoRA without geometric inductive biases, epipolar constraints, or specialized 3D token representations.

Coarse evaluation thresholds: The evaluation metric accepts numerical scalar/vector predictions if the error is within a relatively generous 20% tolerance of the ground truth L2 norm (and 5% image width for coordinates). Reporting standard continuous regression metrics (e.g., MAE, RMSE, median rotation/translation errors) would provide clearer insight into the model's actual metric precision.

Preliminary analysis of emergent phenomena: The claim regarding emergent abilities on the 'Hard' visual correspondence task is based on a single restricted setting and lacks a deeper exploration across continuous model scales and diverse difficult spatial tasks.

strengths: Addresses a crucial and timely bottleneck in multimodal large language models (MLLMs): expanding spatial reasoning from static single-image scenarios to multi-frame dynamic 3D/4D environments (including relative depth, visual correspondence, camera pose changes, and object motion).

Presents a rigorous and scalable automated data curation pipeline (MultiSPA) generating over 27M samples across 26 subtasks, incorporating thoughtful engineering solutions such as overlap-ratio binning, BFS-based minimum-coverage sets, and rigid-body motion clustering.

Comprehensive experimental validation demonstrating substantial gains over strong base models, specialized spatial VLMs (e.g., SpatialRGPT), and frontier proprietary models (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.0, Claude-3.5).

Good cross-domain generalization demonstrated on external benchmarks (BLINK, ERQA, CVBench-3D, synthetic 3RScan) while maintaining parity on standard non-spatial VQA benchmarks without catastrophic forgetting.

Thorough ablation and analytical studies highlighting multi-task synergy across spatial primitives, the impact of tuning vision encoders versus LLM backbones, and potential utility as a multi-frame reward annotator in robotics.
weaknesses: The data generation sources are primarily restricted to indoor environments (ScanNet, Aria Digital Twin, Panoptic Studio). The absence of outdoor or large-scale driving/aerial scenes limits the empirical claim of general-purpose spatial perception for robotics and autonomous driving.

The core framework and training are largely confined to pairwise (two-frame) comparisons. While Table 14 tests multi-frame inference, the model does not truly perform native spatio-temporal reasoning across long video sequences or arbitrary multi-view camera rigs.

The 'emergence' hypothesis in Section 4.3 is backed by limited empirical data points (comparing only 8B, 13B, and 26B models with differing visual encoder architectures), making the claim of emergent behavior somewhat speculative.

Baselines on numerical coordinate/vector extraction frequently suffer from format mismatch and refusal issues. Although GPT-4 post-processing is applied, comparing an instruction-tuned model directly on custom formats against zero-shot frontier models may partially reflect format-adherence discrepancies rather than pure spatial capability differences.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely gap in multimodal foundation models: expanding spatial reasoning from static single-image settings to multi-frame 3D/4D spatial understanding (e.g., relative camera motion, visual correspondence, dynamic object motion, metric object size).

Presents a comprehensive, automated data generation engine leveraging calibrated 3D/4D datasets (ScanNet, ADT, Panoptic Studio via TAPVid3D) with well-designed mechanisms such as overlap binning, rigid body segmentation, and BFS-based minimal coverage set search.

Extensive benchmarking and evaluation across 26 subtasks, comparing against open-source models, single-frame spatial VLMs (SpatialRGPT), and state-of-the-art proprietary models (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.0, Claude-3.5), showing significant quantitative and qualitative improvements.

Solid validation of generalizability and preservation of foundation capabilities: demonstrates strong zero-shot transfer to external benchmarks (BLINK, ERQA, unseen 3RScan data) without degrading performance on general multimodal benchmarks (POPE, VizWiz, MMMU, MMStar).
Valuable empirical insights on cross-task synergy (e.g., visual correspondence and depth aiding camera/object movement perception) and scalability with parameter count and tuning strategies.
weaknesses: The claim regarding 'emergent behavior' in Section 4.3 is relatively weak and overstated; the difference in performance between 8B/13B and 26B on the hard correspondence task appears to be standard capacity-dependent underfitting/generalization rather than an abrupt emergent capability.

The dataset and training primarily focus on image pairs (two frames) rather than longer video sequences or multi-view sets. While Table 14 tests inserting intermediate frames for camera direction, deeper multi-view reasoning and trajectory understanding remain largely unexplored.

Reliance on indoor calibrated datasets (ScanNet, ADT, Panoptic Studio) introduces domain restrictions, potentially limiting generalization to in-the-wild, outdoor, or highly dynamic environments with complex lighting and non-rigid deformations.

Quantitative vector and coordinate estimation performance remains relatively modest for the standard 8B LoRA baseline (e.g., 18% on camera translation vector and 12.92% on object movement vector in Table 2), indicating that high-precision metric spatial regression in MLLMs remains challenging without full model tuning or larger scales.

strengths: Addresses a prominent and timely gap in multimodal foundation models: extending spatial intelligence from static, single-image reasoning (e.g., SpatialVLM, SpatialRGPT) to multi-frame and dynamic spatial perception (depth, visual correspondence, relative camera motion, and object displacement).

Presents a scalable and carefully designed data curation pipeline (MultiSPA) producing over 27M question-answer pairs with rich grounding modalities (coordinates, visual points, semantic labels) and diverse quantitative outputs (scalars, 2D coordinates, 3D vectors). The overlap-binning and rigid-body clustering strategies ensure balanced motion and view distributions.

Extensive empirical validation demonstrating significant gains over both base open-source models (InternVL2) and proprietary systems (GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) on multi-frame spatial tasks, while showing that general multimodal capabilities (POPE, MathVista, MMStar, MMMU) do not suffer catastrophic forgetting.

Strong out-of-domain transfer demonstrated on external benchmarks (BLINK, ERQA, CVBench-3D, and synthetic 3RScan views) and competitive comparisons against specialized 3D perception models (VGGT, LoFTR, Depth Anything).

Valuable analytical experiments detailing multi-task synergies (showing that cross-task spatial data mutually reinforce performance) and fine-tuning configurations (such as the impact of updating vision encoder weights for fine-grained 3D tasks).
weaknesses: The core data generation and fine-tuning setups are predominantly framed around image pairs (two frames); although Appendix L briefly tests inserting 1–4 intermediate frames, true multi-view or long-horizon spatio-temporal reasoning remains relatively unexplored.

Training data relies heavily on existing structured indoor datasets (ScanNet, TAPVid-3D/ADT/Panoptic Studio), which presents domain limitations for outdoor scenes, varying weather/lighting conditions, and dynamic real-world robotic environments.

The claim of 'emergent spatial understanding' in Section 4.3 is supported by only a single small experiment comparing 8B, 13B, and 26B models on a hard distractor setup; this may simply reflect gradual capacity scaling or differing architectural bottlenecks rather than genuine emergence.

Evaluation relies heavily on thresholded binary accuracy metrics (e.g., relative L2 norm <= 0.2, coordinate error <= 5% image width); reporting continuous metrics standard in 3D vision (such as Mean Absolute Error in mm, Root Mean Square Error, and End-Point Error in pixels) would provide a clearer diagnostic view of calibration and precision.
